newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Shipping firms plan terminal charges at Colombo.
newsitem.headline: Shipping firms plan terminal charges at Colombo.

text.p: Shipping lines calling at Colombo port plan to start collecting shore-based charges on Sri Lankan exports from October to help offset falling freight rates and rising costs, shipping officials said on Tuesday.

"We want to impose a terminal handling charge (THC) on export containers as per international practice since we incur this cost now and shipping lines are becoming very cost conscious," said Faizer Hashim, chairman of the Ceylon Association of Ships' Agents (CASA).
Colombo, south Asia's trans-shipment hub, is the only port where the terminal handling charge is not imposed on export containers, he told Reuters.
The move has been opposed by the Indian Ocean island's exporters, who say it will raise their costs as they will be unable to recover the charge from buyers.

Gordon de Silva, chairman of the Shippers' Council representing exporters, told Reuters they were prepared to pay the new charge if it was included in an all-inclusive frieght rate since the money could then be recovered from buyers.
Hashim said they want to charge $61.35 per 20-foot container and $97.85 per 40-foot container from October 1.
Shipping analysts said shipping lines were worried about rising costs and low freight rates in Colombo because of more competition.
"We see a massive fall in freight rates," de Silva said.
Shipping lines with big vessels carrying 4,500 containers prefer to pick up cargo at Colombo even at low rates rather than sail with empty slots, he said.
Freight on garment exports to Europe has plunged to $650 per 20-foot container from $1,820 in 1989, analysts said.
Trans-shipment traffic in the first half of 1996 rose 17.4 percent to 416,304 containers, while domestic import-export traffic rose just 0.2 percent to 159,211 units, they said.
"This is a clear indication foreign lines call in Colombo not to carry the small Sri Lankan export cargo but the massive Indian subcontinent traffic," Hashim said.
